slides.text: Go gives every function its own copy of each argument. In this module you see how a pointer parameter lets a function change the caller's variable, how a function can return a pointer, and which parts are still copies.

A parameter is a new variable that holds a copy of the argument. Changing it never touches the caller's variable.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
caller: score = 50
call addBonus(copy of score)
inside: copy = 60
caller: score is still 50

slides.text:
To change the caller's variable, pass its address. The parameter type becomes `*int`, the call passes `&score`, and the body writes through `*score`.

The address is copied too, but both copies lead to the same variable.

slides.text: A function can return the address of its own local variable. Go keeps that variable alive while a pointer to it exists, and every call makes a new one.
A pointer parameter is a copy of the pointer. Writing through it changes the caller's variable. Assigning a new address to it only moves the copy.
slides.code:
*p = 1     // changes the variable
p = other  // only the copy moves
